summary: Ezekiel 26 (21 verses) continues the story of glory. Starting with 'In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
He will tread down all your streets with the hoofs of his horses. He will kill your people with the sword. The pillars of your strength will go down to the ground.
I will make you a terror, and you will no more have any being. Though you are sought for, yet you will never be found again,’ says the Lord Yahweh.”

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 26?
questions.answer: In 21 verses, this chapter ezekiel 26 (21 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with 'in the eleventh year, in the first of the month, yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 26 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'glory' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Visible weight of God's presence and honor. In this chapter, it appears in context of glory. For a first-time reader: think of it as visible weight of god's presence and honor, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 20 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'then I will bring you down with those who descend into the pit, to the people of old time, and will make you dwell in the lower parts of the earth, in the places that are desolate ...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
